book_desc_summary: Oliver Twist is born into a life of poverty and misfortune in a workhouse in an unnamed town (although when originally published in Bentley's Miscellany in 1837 the town was called Mudfog and said to be within 70 miles north of London - in reality this is the location of the town of Northampton). Orphaned almost from his first breath by his mother’s death in childbirth and his father’s unexplained absence, Oliver is meagerly provided for under the terms of the Poor Law, and spends the first nine years of his life at a baby farm in the 'care' of a woman named Mrs. Mann. Oliver is brought up with little food and few comforts. Around the time of Oliver's ninth birthday, Mr. Bumble, a parish beadle, removes Oliver from the baby farm and puts him to work picking oakum at the main workhouse. Oliver, who toils with very little food, remains in the workhouse for six months. One day, the desperately hungry boys decide to draw lots; the loser must ask for another portion of gruel. The task falls to Oliver, who at the next meal tremblingly comes forward, bowl in hand, and makes his famous request: "Please, sir, I want some more." A great uproar ensues. The board of well-fed gentlemen who administer the workhouse hypocritically offer five pounds to any person wishing to take on the boy as an apprentice. A brutal chimney sweep almost claims Oliver, however, when he begs despairingly not to be sent away with "that dreadful man", a kindly old magistrate refuses to sign the indentures. Later, Mr. Sowerberry, an undertaker employed by the parish, took Oliver into his service. He treats Oliver better, and because of the boy's sorrowful countenance, uses him as a mourner at children’s funerals. However, Mr. Sowerberry is in an unhappy marriage, and his wife takes an immediate dislike to Oliver — primarily because her husband seems to like him — and loses few opportunities to underfeed and mistreat him. He also suffers torment at the hands of Noah Claypole, an oafish but bullying fellow apprentice and "charity boy" who is jealous of Oliver’s promotion to mute, and Charlotte, the Sowerberrys' maidservant, who is in love with Noah. One day, in an attempt to bait Oliver, Noah insults Oliver's biological mother, calling her "a regular right-down bad ‘un". Oliver flies into a rage, attacking and even beating the much bigger boy. Mrs. Sowerberry takes Noah’s side, helps him to subdue, punching, and beating Oliver, and later compels her husband and Mr. Bumble, who has been sent for in the aftermath of the fight, into beating Oliver again. Once Oliver is sent to his room for the night, he does something that he hadn't done since babyhood — he breaks down and weeps. Alone that night, Oliver finally decides to run away, and, "He remembered to have seen the waggons, as they went out, toiling up the hill. He took the same route," until a well-placed milestone sets his wandering feet towards London. During his journey to London, Oliver encounters Jack Dawkins, a pickpocket more commonly known by the nickname the "Artful Dodger", although Oliver's innocent nature prevents him from recognising this hint that the boy may be dishonest. Dodger provides Oliver with a free meal and tells him of a gentleman in London who will "give him lodgings for nothing, and never ask for change". Grateful for the unexpected assistance, Oliver follows Dodger to the "old gentleman"'s residence. In this way, Oliver unwittingly falls in with an infamous Jewish criminal known as Fagin, the so-called gentleman of whom the Artful Dodger spoke. Ensnared, Oliver lives with Fagin and his gang of juvenile pickpockets in their lair at Saffron Hill for some time, unaware of their criminal occupations. He believes they make wallets and handkerchiefs. Later, Oliver naïvely goes out to "make handkerchiefs" because of no income coming in, with two of Fagin’s underlings: The Artful Dodger and a boy of a humorous nature named Charley Bates. Oliver realises too late that their real mission is to pick pockets. Dodger and Charley steal the handkerchief of an old gentleman named Mr. Brownlow, and promptly flee. When he finds his handkerchief missing, Mr. Brownlow turns round, sees Oliver, and pursues him. Others join the chase and Oliver is caught and taken before the magistrate. Curiously, Mr. Brownlow has second thoughts about the boy—he seems reluctant to believe he is a pickpocket. To the judge's evident disappointment, a bookstall holder who saw Dodger commit the crime clears Oliver, who, by now actually ill, faints in the courtroom. Mr. Brownlow takes Oliver home and, along with his housekeeper Mrs. Bedwin, cares for him. Oliver stays with Mr. Brownlow, recovers rapidly, and blossoms from the unaccustomed kindness. His bliss, however, is interrupted when Fagin, fearing Oliver might "peach" on his criminal gang, decides that Oliver must be brought back to his hideout. When Mr. Brownlow sends Oliver out to pay for some books, one of the gang, a young girl named Nancy, whom Oliver had previously met at Fagin's, accosts him with help from her abusive lover, a brutal robber named Bill Sikes, and Oliver is quickly bundled back to Fagin's lair. The thieves take the five-pound note Mr. Brownlow had entrusted to him, and strip him of his fine new clothes. Oliver, dismayed, flees and attempts to call for police assistance, but is ruthlessly dragged back by the Dodger, Charley and Fagin. Nancy, however, is sympathetic towards Oliver and saves him from beatings by Fagin and Sikes. In a renewed attempt to draw Oliver into a life of crime, Fagin forces him to participate in a burglary. Nancy reluctantly assists in recruiting him, all the while assuring the boy that she will help him if she can. Sikes, after threatening to kill him if he does not cooperate, sends Oliver through a small window and orders him to unlock the front door. The robbery goes wrong, however, and Oliver is shot and wounded in his left arm. After being abandoned by Sikes, the wounded Oliver ends up under the care of the people he was supposed to rob: Miss Rose and her guardian Mrs. Maylie Meanwhile, a mysterious man named Monks has found Fagin and is plotting with him to destroy Oliver's reputation. Monks denounces Fagin's failure to turn Oliver into a criminal and the two of them agree on a plan to make sure he does not find out about his past. Monks is apparently related to Oliver in some manner, although it's not mentioned until later. Back in Oliver's hometown, Mr. Bumble married Ms. Corney, the wealthy matron of the workhouse, only to find himself in an unhappy marriage constantly arguing with his domineering wife. After one such argument, Mr. Bumble walks over to a pub, where he meets Monks, who questions him about Oliver. Bumble informs Monks that he knows someone who can give Monks more information for a price, and later Monks meets secretly with the Bumbles. After Mrs. Bumble has told Monks all she knows, the three arrange to take a locket and ring which had once belonged to Oliver's mother and toss them into a nearby river. Monks relates this to Fagin as part of the plot to destroy Oliver, unaware that Nancy has eavesdropped on their conversation and gone ahead to inform Oliver's benefactors. Nancy, by this time ashamed of her role in Oliver's kidnapping, and fearful for the boy's safety, goes to Rose Maylie and Mr. Brownlow to warn them. She knows that Monks and Fagin are plotting to get their hands on the boy again and holds some secret meetings on the subject with Oliver's benefactors. One night Nancy tries to leave for one of the meetings, but Sikes refuses permission when she doesn't state exactly where she's going. Fagin realizes that Nancy is up to something and resolves to find out what her secret is. Meanwhile, Noah has fallen out with the undertaker Mr. Sowerberry, stolen money from him and fled to London. Charlotte has accompanied him — they are now in a relationship. Using the name "Morris Bolter", he joins Fagin's gang for protection and becomes a practicer of "the kinchen lay" (robbing children) while it is implied that Charlotte becomes a prostitute. During Noah's stay with Fagin, the Artful Dodger is caught with a stolen silver snuff box, convicted (in a very humorous courtroom scene) and transported to Australia. Later, Noah is sent by Fagin to "dodge" (spy on) Nancy, and discovers her secret: she has been meeting secretly with Rose and Mr. Brownlow to discuss how to save Oliver from Fagin and Monks. Fagin angrily passes the information on to Sikes, twisting the story just enough to make it sound as if Nancy had informed on him. Believing Nancy to be a traitor, Sikes beats her to death in a fit of rage and later flees to the countryside to escape from the police. There, Sikes is haunted by visions of Nancy's ghost and increasingly alarmed by news of her murder spreading across the countryside. He flees back to London to find a hiding place, only to be killed when he accidentally hangs himself while attempting to flee across a rooftop from an angry mob. Monks is forced by Mr. Brownlow to divulge his secrets: his real name is Edward Leeford, and he is Oliver's paternal half-brother and, although he is legitimate, he was born of a loveless marriage. Oliver's mother, Agnes, was their father's true love. Mr. Brownlow has a picture of her, and began making inquiries when he noticed a marked resemblance between her face and the face of Oliver. Monks has spent many years searching for his father's child—not to befriend him, but to destroy him (see Henry Fielding's Tom Jones for similar circumstances). Brownlow asks Oliver to give half his inheritance (which proves to be meagre) to Monks because he wants to give him a second chance; and Oliver, being prone to giving second chances, is more than happy to comply. Monks then moves to America, where he squanders his money, reverts to crime, and ultimately dies in prison. Fagin is arrested and condemned to the gallows. On the eve of his hanging, in an emotional scene, Oliver, accompanied by Mr. Brownlow, goes to visit the old reprobate in Newgate Gaol, where Fagin's terror at being hanged has caused him to come down with fever. As Mr. Brownlow and Oliver leave the prison, Fagin screams in terror and despair as a crowd gathers to see his hanging. On a happier note, Rose Maylie turns out to be the long-lost sister of Agnes; she is therefore Oliver's aunt. She marries her long-time sweetheart Harry, and Oliver lives happily with his saviour, Mr. Brownlow. Noah becomes a paid, semi-professional informer to the police. The Bumbles lose their jobs and are reduced to great poverty, eventually ending up in the same workhouse where they originally had lorded it over Oliver and the other boys; and Charley Bates, horrified by Sikes's murder of Nancy, becomes an honest citizen, moves to the country, and works his way up to prosperity.

Mrs. Mann dismisses Oliver's request to write a letter to his friend, but Mr. Bumble intervenes and takes Oliver to the coal cellar. Mr. Bumble then heads to London, where he encounters two complaining paupers and reads an advertisement offering a reward for information about Oliver Twist. Upon reaching Mr. Brownlow's residence, Mr. Bumble meets Mrs. Bedwin, who defends Oliver. In Chapter XIX of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. Fagin and Mr. Sikes meet in a poorly furnished room to discuss their failed attempt to rob Mrs. Corney's house. Despite offering substantial bribes, they were unable to persuade either the male or female servants to assist them. Even Toby Crackit, known for his cunning, was unsuccessful in his attempts. Fagin considers alternative methods but ultimately agrees to try again, offering extra payment if the robbery can be executed from the outside. Sikes is reluctant but accepts the proposal. Nancy, who overhears the conversation, remains silent and attentive. The chapter concludes with Fagin and Sikes making plans for their next attempt. The meeting highlights the tension and mutual distrust between Fagin and Sikes, as well as the ongoing challenges they face in their criminal activities. ###

chapters.summary: In "Oliver Twist," Mr. Fagin and Mr. Sikes discuss their plan to kidnap Oliver Twist. They decide that Nancy will bring Oliver to Fagin the following evening after dark. Fagin manipulates Sikes into agreeing to handle the kidnapping, promising to confirm details later with Toby Crackit. Sikes, becoming intoxicated, falls asleep holding a box of housebreaking tools. Fagin, finding Oliver sleeping on a floor bed, decides to wait until the next day to speak with him. The chapter ends with Fagin's ominous departure, hinting at the impending danger for Oliver.

In Chapter XX of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver wakes up to find new shoes and learns he is to be taken to Mr. William Sikes' residence that night. Fagin warns Oliver to remain silent and follow instructions, while Nancy visits him, revealing she has come from Bill Sikes. She instructs Oliver to accompany her and warns him not to speak unless spoken to, hinting at the necessity of using a pistol if he does. Mr. Sikes arrives and gives Oliver a stern lecture about the consequences of speaking during their planned robbery. After a meal, Nancy instructs Oliver to sleep on a mattress on the floor, while Mr. Sikes goes to bed. Sikes orders Nancy to wake him at exactly five o'clock. The group prepares for a robbery, with Sikes warning Nancy to silence any informants by lethal means if necessary. Oliver, dressed in a handkerchief and cape, is led out by Sikes while Nancy remains motionless by the fire. The weather is stormy, and it is still dark outside when they leave. ###

In Chapter XXI of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. Sikes and Oliver embark on a journey on a gloomy, rainy morning. They navigate through London, encounter a bustling market in Smithfield, and eventually get a ride to Isleworth. After walking through several towns and having a meal, they reach Hampton and spend the night at an old public house. Oliver falls asleep, and when he wakes, Sikes is discussing their next move with another laborer. They agree to be given a ride to Lower Halliford. The journey continues through the countryside, with Oliver becoming increasingly uneasy. They pass Sunbury Church and Shepperton, eventually reaching a dilapidated house near a bridge. Inside, the fear in Oliver's heart intensifies as he believes Sikes intends to murder him, but it turns out they are merely entering the house. The next part of their plan remains unclear. ###

In Chapter XXII of *Oliver Twist*, Bill Sikes and Toby Crackit, along with Barney, enter a dark room where Toby, running a criminal operation, recognizes Oliver as Fagin's boy and comments on his value. Sikes coerces Oliver, who has been drugged, into accompanying them on a burglary in Chertsey. They quickly cross the town and break into a house through a small window, with Sikes threatening Oliver to remain silent. When Oliver hears a commotion and drops the lantern, Sikes drags him out through the window. Sikes discovers Oliver has been shot and instructs someone to bring a shawl. The group is pursued, and the sounds of gunfire and men's shouts are heard as they flee. Oliver becomes increasingly disoriented and eventually stops seeing or hearing anything. The chapter sets the stage for the impending doom of Oliver's situation. ###

In Chapter XXIII of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. Bumble visits the matron, Mrs. Corney, at the workhouse. They discuss the management of out-of-door relief for paupers, with Mr. Bumble suggesting that giving them unwanted items discourages further requests. Mr. Bumble then brings port wine for the infirmary and offers to stay for tea. During their conversation, Mr. Bumble makes flirtatious comments and unexpectedly kisses Mrs. Corney, causing her to lose her voice out of fright. Before she can scream, an old pauper informs them that Old Sally, a resident of the workhouse, is near death and wants to speak to Mrs. Corney. Mrs. Corney leaves to see Old Sally, while Mr. Bumble exhibits odd behavior, including counting utensils and dancing around the table, before settling by the fire in thought. The scene highlights the stark contrast between the comfortable lives of the well-off and the harsh conditions faced by the destitute.

In Chapter XXIV of *Oliver Twist*, a dying woman named Sally lies in a poorhouse, whispering her final words to a matron. She recounts how she once cared for a young woman who arrived at the hospital with injured and soiled feet, giving birth to a boy before dying. Sally confesses to stealing a piece of rich gold from the dead woman, believing it could have helped save her life. The dying woman also mentions that the boy, named Oliver, resembled his mother and that she died asking for friends to be raised for him. Before the matron can gather more information, Sally passes away. The old women, who had been listening, leave to tend to other patients, and the matron departs without further inquiry. ###

In Chapter XXV of *Oliver Twist*, Tom confronts Fagin about his decision not to betray Nancy, who was killed by Bill Sikes. Tom expresses regret and anger at not taking action, but Fagin reassures him that he made the right choice. The group then hears a noise, and the Dodger goes upstairs to investigate. He returns with Toby Crackit, a housebreaker who has been missing. Toby explains that the robbery attempt failed because they were fired upon, and they had to leave the boy behind. Fagin becomes extremely agitated and leaves the house in distress. ###

In Chapter XXVI of *Oliver Twist*, Fagin engages in several key interactions. Initially, he hurries through the streets of London, avoiding main thoroughfares, and eventually reaches Field Lane, a notorious alley known for its criminal activity. There, he meets Mr. Lively, a handkerchief trader, and inquires about Sikes and Barney, learning that neither is present at the Three Cripples public house. Fagin then meets with Monks, who reports that Barney is managing their affairs well. Fagin instructs Monks to meet him the next day instead of immediately. Later, Fagin visits Nancy, who appears drunk and unresponsive. When Fagin mentions Bill (Sikes), Nancy expresses strong dislike for him and the child he left behind, but Fagin threatens to kill Bill if he returns with the child. Fagin also encounters a mysterious stranger, likely Monks, who criticizes his handling of Oliver and suggests the boy should have been kept as a pickpocket. Fagin defends his actions and argues that the girl who has taken an interest in Oliver could be used to make him a thief. The chapter concludes with Monks expressing fear over Oliver's potential death and dismissing a shadow on the wall as his own imagination. Both men part ways, with the time being past one o'clock. The chapter sets the stage for ongoing criminal activities and hints at the complex relationships within Fagin's criminal network. ###

In Chapter XXVII of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. Bumble visits Mrs. Corney at the workhouse, where they discuss their potential marriage and Mr. Bumble's possible rise to power if Mr. Slout, the master, dies. Mrs. Corney agrees to marry Mr. Bumble, and they share affectionate words and a kiss. Mr. Bumble then goes to the undertaker's shop, where he finds Noah and Charlotte in a drunken and intimate situation. Mr. Bumble reprimands them, orders Noah to close the shop, and warns him against speaking further until his master returns. The chapter highlights the moral corruption and social issues within the workhouse and among the lower classes. Additionally, the search for young Oliver Twist continues as he was left in a ditch by Toby Crackit. ###

In Chapter XXVIII of "Oliver Twist," Sikes, a robber, abandons Oliver after an escape attempt with Toby Crackit. Pursued by Mr. Giles, Brittles, and a traveling tinker, Sikes and Toby flee, leaving Oliver alone and injured in a ditch. As morning approaches, the weather worsens, and Oliver remains unconscious and bleeding. Eventually, he wakes up, feeling weak and in pain from a wounded arm. He experiences vivid flashbacks and tries to walk towards a nearby house but is deterred by fear and confusion. Meanwhile, Mr. Giles recounts the burglary attempt and the discovery of Oliver to Brittles and the tinker. Oliver is mistakenly identified as one of the thieves and is brought to Mr. Giles's room, where Brittles and others carefully carry him upstairs for treatment. The young lady present refuses to look at Oliver but insists he be treated kindly. ###

In a well-furnished room, two ladies are having breakfast. The older lady, Mrs. Maylie, is seated in a high-backed chair, dressed in a mix of old and new styles. Her young companion, Rose, is in her late teens, described as pure and beautiful. Mr. Giles, dressed formally in black, stands nearby, looking important. A fat gentleman arrives unexpectedly, causing a commotion, and identifies himself as Dr. Losberne. He expresses shock at a robbery that occurred in the night and rushes upstairs to examine a patient. After a long absence, Dr. Losberne returns and reveals that a boy was shot during the incident. Despite initial reluctance, Mrs. Maylie agrees to see the injured boy in Dr. Losberne's presence. ###

In Chapter XXX of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver, who is ill but determined to recount his story, shares his experiences with Dr. Losberne and Mrs. Maylie, along with her niece Rose. He describes the hardships and injustices he has endured, evoking deep sympathy from his caregivers. Throughout the night, Rose and Mrs. Maylie provide care and comfort to Oliver. Dr. Losberne then goes to confront Mr. Giles and Brittles, planning to secure Oliver's release using his authority. Meanwhile, Mr. Giles, concerned about Oliver's well-being, joins the servants in the kitchen. The doctor questions them about identifying Oliver as the boy seen fleeing the previous night, stressing the importance of their oath. When the Bow Street runners arrive, Brittles explains that he had sent for them earlier, causing frustration for the doctor. The chapter underscores the compassion of the Maylies and the ongoing efforts to secure Oliver's freedom. ###

In Chapter XXXI of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. Losberne and the doctor are discussing the situation of a young boy suspected of involvement in a robbery attempt at the Maylies' house. Mr. Losberne insists the boy is innocent and does not want to reveal his true background to the police, fearing it might not be believed and could complicate matters. The police officers, Mr. Blathers and Mr. Duff, arrive to investigate and question the servants. They find that the pistol used was harmless, and Mr. Giles, the butler, admits he may have mistaken Oliver for the housebreaker's boy. The officers leave for the night, promising to return the next day. Meanwhile, Mr. Losberne and Rose discuss the boy's situation, and the next morning, news arrives that two men and a boy arrested in Kingston were found sleeping under a haystack and not charged with burglary. Despite the initial suspicion, Oliver is cared for by Mrs. Maylie, Rose, and Mr. Losberne, with his prayers bringing blessings to them. ###

In Chapter XXXII of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver, recovering from illness under the care of the Maylies and Rose, expresses gratitude and eagerness to serve them. They plan to take him to the countryside for healing, and Dr. Losberne accompanies him to visit the house where Oliver was held captive by Fagin's gang. Oliver recognizes the house and encounters Sikes, who angrily denies any wrongdoing. Dr. Losberne's impulsive actions lead them back to London, where they learn that Mr. Brownlow and Mrs. Bedwin have moved to the West Indies. Oliver feels deeply disappointed but finds solace in a cottage with Mrs. Maylie and Rose, where he learns to read and write and experiences a peaceful, joyful life. The chapter highlights Oliver's transformation and his growing bond with the Maylies. Dr. Losberne, though impulsive, remains respected by others. ###

In Chapter XXXIII of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver and his friends enjoy a peaceful and vibrant spring in their village. At the Maylie cottage, Rose, Oliver’s cousin, suddenly falls ill with a high fever. Mrs. Maylie, remaining composed, sends Oliver to fetch Dr. Losberne from Chertsey and considers writing to Harry Maylie. Despite her worsening condition, Rose’s aunt maintains her resolve. Oliver, anxious but determined, successfully delivers the letters. On his return, he finds Rose delirious and the medical practitioner pessimistic about her recovery. Throughout the night, Oliver prays and watches over her. The next day, Dr. Losberne confirms the dire prognosis. As the sun shines brightly and flowers bloom, Rose’s condition deteriorates further. Oliver goes to the churchyard, where he weeps and prays for her. A church bell tolls for Rose’s funeral, and a group of mourners, including a mother, enter the church. Back at the cottage, Mrs. Maylie, overwhelmed by grief, pleads for news of Rose. Dr. Losberne reassures her that Rose will recover, and Mrs. Maylie collapses in relief and gratitude. The family anxiously waits for any sign of improvement. ###

In Chapter XXXIV of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver returns home after receiving news that a loved one is improving and brings flowers to decorate the sick room. On his way, he encounters a post-chaise driven by a young man named Harry Maylie, who shows great concern for the patient's condition. Harry and Oliver walk together, and Oliver notices that Harry resembles the patient, who is revealed to be Harry's mother, Mrs. Maylie. Mrs. Maylie discusses the challenges of reconciling her love for Harry with the social stigma of his past actions. Harry expresses his unwavering love for his mother, and Mrs. Maylie encourages him to think carefully about his feelings and the potential consequences. Meanwhile, Oliver continues to feel more hopeful and cheerful, enjoying his time with Dr. Losberne and Harry Maylie, and sharing stories and laughter. Despite this, Oliver has a disturbing dream where he feels back in Fagin's den, and he leaps from the window, shouting for help. ###

In Chapter XXXV of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver informs Mr. Giles and Harry Maylie about spotting Fagin and another man (the "tall man") fleeing into the meadows. After a fruitless search, the group returns to the cottage where Rose is recovering. Harry expresses his deep love for Rose, recounting the emotional turmoil he experienced during her illness. Rose, though touched, rejects his advances, explaining that she must protect her own reputation and that of Harry and his family. She suggests they remain friends but ultimately must part ways. Harry, heartbroken, agrees to respect her decision and requests a meeting within a year. The chapter ends with Rose extending her hand as a final gesture, symbolizing the end of their romantic pursuit. ###

In Chapter XXXVI of *Oliver Twist*, Dr. Losberne discusses Harry Maylie's inconsistent plans with Oliver. Harry decides to travel with Dr. Losberne to London, despite earlier intentions to stay with his mother. Dr. Losberne speculates that Harry's sudden change of heart might be due to political ambitions. Harry asks Oliver to write to him regularly while he is away, promising to share details about his life and family without mentioning it to them. After a brief farewell, Harry and Dr. Losberne depart in a post-chaise, leaving Rose, Harry's mother, watching from the window. She expresses relief that Harry appears happy and hopeful. Despite her outward happiness, tears suggest she feels a mix of emotions. ###

In Chapter XXXVII of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. Bumble, the former beadle and current master of the workhouse, experiences a significant decline in his authority and social standing. Following his marriage to Mrs. Corney, Mr. Bumble's life has changed dramatically, but his newfound power is tested when his wife, Mrs. Bumble, who is living with another man, Mr. Corney, physically assaults him. Humiliated and defeated, Mr. Bumble flees the scene, showcasing his cowardice. Later, he encounters a mysterious stranger who questions him about his past as a beadle and his current role. The stranger, who seems suspicious and sarcastic, reveals that he knows about a woman named Sally, who nursed Oliver's mother during childbirth, and instructs Mr. Bumble to bring her to a specified address the next evening. The stranger, who refers to himself as "Monks," gives Mr. Bumble an address by the water-side and insists on secrecy. Before leaving, the stranger tells Mr. Bumble to be referred to as "Monks." The chapter highlights Mr. Bumble's fall from grace and the importance of outward symbols of status. ###

In Chapter XXXVIII of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. and Mrs. Bumble, along with Mr. Monks, meet in a dilapidated building during a stormy evening to discuss a secret. Monks inquires about a trinket stolen from a dead woman named "old Sally," which Mrs. Bumble confirms was a pawnbroker's receipt for a gold locket containing hair and a wedding ring inscribed with "Agnes." The locket was intended as a memento for her child, Oliver Twist. Monks offers 25 pounds for more information, but Mrs. Bumble refuses to provide any additional details. Monks then drops the locket into a nearby river and departs with a boy. Mr. and Mrs. Bumble leave the premises, leaving Monks alone. ###

In Chapter XXXIX of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. William Sikes returns to Fagin's hideout, where he finds himself in a poor condition, having been ill for several weeks. Fagin and the Artful Dodger (John Dawkins) bring him a bundle containing various delicacies and alcohol, which he initially resents but eventually accepts, showing signs of improvement. Nancy, also ill, assists Sikes. Fagin gives Sikes £3 4s 6d, and Sikes insists that Nancy go to fetch the money to ensure it is brought. Meanwhile, Toby Crackit visits Fagin's den after winning a game of cards, boasting about his victory and leaving with a swagger. Mr. Chitling expresses satisfaction with his acquaintance despite losing money. Fagin sends the boys, Dodger and Charley, on a "lay," while Nancy overhears a conversation between Fagin and Monks, a mysterious man. Nancy becomes agitated and runs away from Sikes, returning to the house where she left the housebreaker. She then hurries to Miss Maylie's hotel, where she waits anxiously before being allowed to see Miss Maylie. Nancy's urgency and determination suggest she has a pressing reason to meet Miss Maylie. ###

In Chapter XL of *Oliver Twist*, Nancy, a former associate of Fagin, visits Rose Maylie to reveal crucial information about Oliver's past. Nancy mentions that Monks, who has been plotting against Oliver, refers to him as "his brother" and believes Oliver's fate is predetermined. Nancy expresses her desire to return to her criminal associates, despite her recent change of heart and feelings of guilt. Rose, moved by Nancy's plea, offers to keep her secret and suggests meeting again to discuss further. Nancy, however, refuses any financial assistance and leaves, expressing deep regret and a sense of fatalism about her situation. The encounter leaves Rose emotionally overwhelmed as she tries to process the information and decide on her next steps. ### Final Combined Summary: In Chapter XL of *Oliver Twist*, Nancy, a former associate of Fagin, visits Rose Maylie to reveal crucial information about Oliver's past. Nancy mentions that Monks, who has been plotting against Oliver, refers to him as "his brother" and believes Oliver's fate is predetermined. Nancy expresses her desire to return to her criminal associates, despite her recent change of heart and feelings of guilt. Rose, moved by Nancy's plea, offers to keep her secret and suggests meeting again to discuss further. Nancy, however, refuses any financial assistance and leaves, expressing deep regret and a sense of fatalism about her situation. The encounter leaves Rose emotionally overwhelmed as she tries to process the information and decide on her next steps. ###

In Chapter XLI of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. Brownlow returns to the Maylie residence after hearing about Oliver's safety and is pleased to learn that Rose Maylie has found him. Mr. Grimwig, initially skeptical, becomes emotional and affectionate towards Oliver. Mrs. Bedwin, Oliver's nurse, is overjoyed to see him. Mr. Brownlow hears Rose's account of her meeting with Nancy, who is revealed to be involved in Oliver's rescue. Dr. Losberne is furious and considers punishing Nancy, but Mr. Brownlow insists on proceeding carefully to uncover Oliver's parentage and rightful inheritance. They plan to meet Nancy on Sunday night to gather information about Monks, avoiding legal involvement. Mr. Brownlow proposes bringing in his friend Grimwig for assistance. The group decides to stay in town while pursuing the investigation and avoids discussing Mr. Brownlow's absence. They plan to inform Oliver about their plans later. The chapter ends with the group moving to the supper room. ###

In Chapter XLII of "Oliver Twist," Noah Claypole and Charlotte arrive at the Three Cripples inn in London after a journey. They are served by a young Jewish bartender named Barney, who shows them a room directly behind the bar. Noah, suspicious and impatient, is wary of being recognized. Fagin overhears their conversation and approaches, offering them protection and a place in his criminal enterprise. He describes a successful operation run by a friend with high society connections. Noah agrees to meet Fagin's friend the next morning under the name "Mr. Morris Bolter," while adopting a superior attitude towards Charlotte. The encounter sets the stage for their integration into the criminal world. ###

In Chapter XLIII of *Oliver Twist*, Fagin discusses the importance of self-interest and mutual trust within their criminal group, emphasizing that each member depends on the others to maintain their operations. He reveals that the Artful Dodger, one of their key members, has been caught attempting to pick a pocket and is facing potential transportation for life. Fagin reacts angrily to Charley Bates' disappointment over the Dodger's arrest, defending the Dodger's reputation and emphasizing his skill and importance to the group. Charley Bates expresses sorrow over the Dodger's imprisonment, feeling that he lacks honor and glory. Fagin reassures him that the Dodger will still be recognized for his talents and plans to keep him in comfortable conditions. Mr. Bolter, also known as Noah Claypole, agrees to visit the police station disguised as a waggoner to gather information, while Charley Bates remains frustrated. The chapter also describes the squalid conditions of the Bow Street Magistrates' Court, where the Dodger is brought before the judge and behaves arrogantly, refusing to cooperate with the witness. Noah returns to Master Bates to report the outcome, and the two then inform Mr. Fagin of the situation. ###

In Chapter XLIV of *Oliver Twist*, Nancy, involved in Fagin's criminal activities, feels conflicted about a secret that could endanger her friends. She decides to meet Rose Maylie despite her reluctance. On a Sunday night, Sikes and Fagin discuss potential criminal activities while Nancy tries to leave for some fresh air. Sikes becomes suspicious and locks her in a small room, questioning and threatening her. Nancy pleads to be released but is held down

In Chapter XLV of *Oliver Twist*, Fagin employs Noah Claypole on a secret mission. Noah arrives late for breakfast and complains about the lack of time to eat. Fagin commends Noah's performance from the previous day, mentioning he earned six shillings and ninepence. Noah asks about a reward, and Fagin promises a pound if Noah completes the task successfully. Fagin explains that Noah needs to spy on a fellow criminal, a young woman who has made new friends. Noah agrees to the task, eager for the reward. Over the next six nights, Noah waits for instructions from Fagin, who repeatedly returns disappointed. On the seventh night, Fagin reveals that the woman will be out that evening and instructs Noah to follow her. They arrive at a public house where Noah climbs up to observe the woman. After adjusting the lighting, Noah identifies the woman clearly. He follows her as she leaves the pub, maintaining a safe distance and noting her movements. The woman seems to gain confidence as she walks, and Noah continues to follow her until she reaches her destination. ###

In Chapter XLVI of *Oliver Twist*, Nancy meets with Mr. Brownlow on London Bridge, where she expresses distress over seeing "real coffins" and discusses her past with a young lady (possibly Agnes). Nancy recounts a distinctive scar on Oliver's neck, confirming Mr. Brownlow's suspicions that Oliver is the boy he seeks. Mr. Brownlow attempts to persuade Nancy to leave her criminal life and join him, offering her a chance at a better future. Nancy initially resists but ultimately agrees to leave, taking a keepsake from the young lady (a purse and a handkerchief). As Nancy departs, Noah Claypole informs Fagin about their encounter. ###

In Chapter XLVII of *Oliver Twist*, Fagin, agitated by Nancy's betrayal to the authorities, confronts Sikes after Noah has fallen asleep. Noah confirms that Nancy met with two strangers and provided them with information about the gang, including details about Monks and the meeting place. Fagin's distress intensifies as Noah mentions that Nancy was prevented from attending a meeting by Sikes. Sikes, enraged, leaves the house and returns to find Nancy half-dressed. He accuses her of being watched and threatened, and she pleads for mercy, offering to leave with him. However, Sikes strikes her with a club, causing her to fall and bleed profusely. She prays for mercy before losing consciousness. Sikes then departs the room. Fagin remains agitated and watches over Noah, who is asleep on a mattress. ###

In Chapter XLVIII of *Oliver Twist*, Sikes, the murderer of Nancy, flees the crime scene after disposing of evidence and burns the murder weapon. He moves through various London locations, including Islington, Highgate, Hampstead Heath, and Hatfield, while feeling increasingly paranoid and haunted by visions of Nancy. At a small public house in Hatfield, he buys a stain remover from a peddler and overhears a conversation about a recent murder in Spitalfields, which intensifies his fear. Sikes finds temporary relief in a shed but is later drawn to a fire, where the commotion helps distract him from his guilt. book_desc_summary: Oliver Twist is born into a life of poverty and misfortune in a workhouse in an unnamed town (although when originally published in Bentley's Miscellany in 1837 the town was called Mudfog and said to be within 70 miles north of London - in reality this is the location of the town of Northampton). Orphaned almost from his first breath by his mother’s death in childbirth and his father’s unexplained absence, Oliver is meagerly provided for under the terms of the Poor Law, and spends the first nine years of his life at a baby farm in the 'care' of a woman named Mrs. Mann. Oliver is brought up with little food and few comforts. Around the time of Oliver's ninth birthday, Mr. Bumble, a parish beadle, removes Oliver from the baby farm and puts him to work picking oakum at the main workhouse. Oliver, who toils with very little food, remains in the workhouse for six months. One day, the desperately hungry boys decide to draw lots; the loser must ask for another portion of gruel. The task falls to Oliver, who at the next meal tremblingly comes forward, bowl in hand, and makes his famous request: "Please, sir, I want some more." A great uproar ensues. The board of well-fed gentlemen who administer the workhouse hypocritically offer five pounds to any person wishing to take on the boy as an apprentice. A brutal chimney sweep almost claims Oliver, however, when he begs despairingly not to be sent away with "that dreadful man", a kindly old magistrate refuses to sign the indentures. Later, Mr. Sowerberry, an undertaker employed by the parish, took Oliver into his service. He treats Oliver better, and because of the boy's sorrowful countenance, uses him as a mourner at children’s funerals. However, Mr. Sowerberry is in an unhappy marriage, and his wife takes an immediate dislike to Oliver — primarily because her husband seems to like him — and loses few opportunities to underfeed and mistreat him. He also suffers torment at the hands of Noah Claypole, an oafish but bullying fellow apprentice and "charity boy" who is jealous of Oliver’s promotion to mute, and Charlotte, the Sowerberrys' maidservant, who is in love with Noah. One day, in an attempt to bait Oliver, Noah insults Oliver's biological mother, calling her "a regular right-down bad ‘un". Oliver flies into a rage, attacking and even beating the much bigger boy. Mrs. Sowerberry takes Noah’s side, helps him to subdue, punching, and beating Oliver, and later compels her husband and Mr. Bumble, who has been sent for in the aftermath of the fight, into beating Oliver again. Once Oliver is sent to his room for the night, he does something that he hadn't done since babyhood — he breaks down and weeps. Alone that night, Oliver finally decides to run away, and, "He remembered to have seen the waggons, as they went out, toiling up the hill. He took the same route," until a well-placed milestone sets his wandering feet towards London. During his journey to London, Oliver encounters Jack Dawkins, a pickpocket more commonly known by the nickname the "Artful Dodger", although Oliver's innocent nature prevents him from recognising this hint that the boy may be dishonest. Dodger provides Oliver with a free meal and tells him of a gentleman in London who will "give him lodgings for nothing, and never ask for change". Grateful for the unexpected assistance, Oliver follows Dodger to the "old gentleman"'s residence. In this way, Oliver unwittingly falls in with an infamous Jewish criminal known as Fagin, the so-called gentleman of whom the Artful Dodger spoke. Ensnared, Oliver lives with Fagin and his gang of juvenile pickpockets in their lair at Saffron Hill for some time, unaware of their criminal occupations. He believes they make wallets and handkerchiefs. Later, Oliver naïvely goes out to "make handkerchiefs" because of no income coming in, with two of Fagin’s underlings: The Artful Dodger and a boy of a humorous nature named Charley Bates. Oliver realises too late that their real mission is to pick pockets. Dodger and Charley steal the handkerchief of an old gentleman named Mr. Brownlow, and promptly flee. When he finds his handkerchief missing, Mr. Brownlow turns round, sees Oliver, and pursues him. Others join the chase and Oliver is caught and taken before the magistrate. Curiously, Mr. Brownlow has second thoughts about the boy—he seems reluctant to believe he is a pickpocket. To the judge's evident disappointment, a bookstall holder who saw Dodger commit the crime clears Oliver, who, by now actually ill, faints in the courtroom. Mr. Brownlow takes Oliver home and, along with his housekeeper Mrs. Bedwin, cares for him. Oliver stays with Mr. Brownlow, recovers rapidly, and blossoms from the unaccustomed kindness. His bliss, however, is interrupted when Fagin, fearing Oliver might "peach" on his criminal gang, decides that Oliver must be brought back to his hideout. When Mr. Brownlow sends Oliver out to pay for some books, one of the gang, a young girl named Nancy, whom Oliver had previously met at Fagin's, accosts him with help from her abusive lover, a brutal robber named Bill Sikes, and Oliver is quickly bundled back to Fagin's lair. The thieves take the five-pound note Mr. Brownlow had entrusted to him, and strip him of his fine new clothes. Oliver, dismayed, flees and attempts to call for police assistance, but is ruthlessly dragged back by the Dodger, Charley and Fagin. Nancy, however, is sympathetic towards Oliver and saves him from beatings by Fagin and Sikes. In a renewed attempt to draw Oliver into a life of crime, Fagin forces him to participate in a burglary. Nancy reluctantly assists in recruiting him, all the while assuring the boy that she will help him if she can. Sikes, after threatening to kill him if he does not cooperate, sends Oliver through a small window and orders him to unlock the front door. The robbery goes wrong, however, and Oliver is shot and wounded in his left arm. After being abandoned by Sikes, the wounded Oliver ends up under the care of the people he was supposed to rob: Miss Rose and her guardian Mrs. Maylie Meanwhile, a mysterious man named Monks has found Fagin and is plotting with him to destroy Oliver's reputation. Monks denounces Fagin's failure to turn Oliver into a criminal and the two of them agree on a plan to make sure he does not find out about his past. Monks is apparently related to Oliver in some manner, although it's not mentioned until later. Back in Oliver's hometown, Mr. Bumble married Ms. Corney, the wealthy matron of the workhouse, only to find himself in an unhappy marriage constantly arguing with his domineering wife. After one such argument, Mr. Bumble walks over to a pub, where he meets Monks, who questions him about Oliver. Bumble informs Monks that he knows someone who can give Monks more information for a price, and later Monks meets secretly with the Bumbles. After Mrs. Bumble has told Monks all she knows, the three arrange to take a locket and ring which had once belonged to Oliver's mother and toss them into a nearby river. Monks relates this to Fagin as part of the plot to destroy Oliver, unaware that Nancy has eavesdropped on their conversation and gone ahead to inform Oliver's benefactors. Nancy, by this time ashamed of her role in Oliver's kidnapping, and fearful for the boy's safety, goes to Rose Maylie and Mr. Brownlow to warn them. She knows that Monks and Fagin are plotting to get their hands on the boy again and holds some secret meetings on the subject with Oliver's benefactors. One night Nancy tries to leave for one of the meetings, but Sikes refuses permission when she doesn't state exactly where she's going. Fagin realizes that Nancy is up to something and resolves to find out what her secret is. Meanwhile, Noah has fallen out with the undertaker Mr. Sowerberry, stolen money from him and fled to London. Charlotte has accompanied him — they are now in a relationship. Using the name "Morris Bolter", he joins Fagin's gang for protection and becomes a practicer of "the kinchen lay" (robbing children) while it is implied that Charlotte becomes a prostitute. During Noah's stay with Fagin, the Artful Dodger is caught with a stolen silver snuff box, convicted (in a very humorous courtroom scene) and transported to Australia. Later, Noah is sent by Fagin to "dodge" (spy on) Nancy, and discovers her secret: she has been meeting secretly with Rose and Mr. Brownlow to discuss how to save Oliver from Fagin and Monks. Fagin angrily passes the information on to Sikes, twisting the story just enough to make it sound as if Nancy had informed on him. Believing Nancy to be a traitor, Sikes beats her to death in a fit of rage and later flees to the countryside to escape from the police. There, Sikes is haunted by visions of Nancy's ghost and increasingly alarmed by news of her murder spreading across the countryside. He flees back to London to find a hiding place, only to be killed when he accidentally hangs himself while attempting to flee across a rooftop from an angry mob. Monks is forced by Mr. Brownlow to divulge his secrets: his real name is Edward Leeford, and he is Oliver's paternal half-brother and, although he is legitimate, he was born of a loveless marriage. Oliver's mother, Agnes, was their father's true love. Mr. Brownlow has a picture of her, and began making inquiries when he noticed a marked resemblance between her face and the face of Oliver. Monks has spent many years searching for his father's child—not to befriend him, but to destroy him (see Henry Fielding's Tom Jones for similar circumstances). Brownlow asks Oliver to give half his inheritance (which proves to be meagre) to Monks because he wants to give him a second chance; and Oliver, being prone to giving second chances, is more than happy to comply. Monks then moves to America, where he squanders his money, reverts to crime, and ultimately dies in prison. Fagin is arrested and condemned to the gallows. On the eve of his hanging, in an emotional scene, Oliver, accompanied by Mr. Brownlow, goes to visit the old reprobate in Newgate Gaol, where Fagin's terror at being hanged has caused him to come down with fever. As Mr. Brownlow and Oliver leave the prison, Fagin screams in terror and despair as a crowd gathers to see his hanging. On a happier note, Rose Maylie turns out to be the long-lost sister of Agnes; she is therefore Oliver's aunt. She marries her long-time sweetheart Harry, and Oliver lives happily with his saviour, Mr. Brownlow. Noah becomes a paid, semi-professional informer to the police. The Bumbles lose their jobs and are reduced to great poverty, eventually ending up in the same workhouse where they originally had lorded it over Oliver and the other boys; and Charley Bates, horrified by Sikes's murder of Nancy, becomes an honest citizen, moves to the country, and works his way up to prosperity.

chapters.summary: **Oliver Twist** by Charles Dickens is a novel that follows the life of an orphan named Oliver Twist from his birth in a workhouse to his adventures in London. The story begins with Oliver's birth and early years in the workhouse, where he grows up under harsh conditions. He eventually leaves the workhouse and finds himself in various situations, including being offered jobs and befriending a group of criminals led by Fagin. Oliver's journey takes him through different parts of London, where he encounters various characters such as Mr. Brownlow, Nancy, and Monks. He faces numerous challenges and dangers, including being involved in a burglary and narrowly escaping capture. Throughout the novel, Oliver's character develops as he navigates the complexities of his life, ultimately leading to a resolution involving his true identity and the people who care for him. The narrative includes several key events such as Oliver's time with Fagin and his friends, his interactions with Mr. Brownlow, and his eventual reunion with his long-lost family. The book concludes with a dramatic confrontation between Monks and Mr. Brownlow, followed by a pursuit and escape, and ends with Fagin's death. Overall, the novel explores themes of poverty, injustice, and redemption. ###

In a workhouse in an unnamed town, Oliver Twist is born on a day and date unspecified. Due to initial breathing difficulties, there is doubt about his survival. After a struggle, he begins to breathe and cry, alerting the workhouse to his presence. A young woman, who had been lying ill, dies after holding and kissing the newborn. The surgeon and nurse, who are present, note that she had no wedding ring, indicating she was unmarried. The nurse dresses the infant in old, calico robes, marking him as a parish child and an orphan. In Chapter II of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver, an orphan, is sent to a harsh workhouse where he faces inadequate food and care under the mismanagement of Mrs. Mann. On his ninth birthday, Oliver is locked in the coal cellar for being hungry, and Mr. Bumble, the beadle, takes him back to the main workhouse. There, the board decides Oliver will start picking oakum the next day. Despite the poor conditions, Oliver falls asleep. The board implements a cost-cutting measure, reducing food rations, which leads to severe malnutrition among the residents. When Oliver asks for more gruel, he is confined, and a reward is offered for taking him in as an apprentice. The board believes his future will be bleak, but the narrative suggests otherwise. In Chapter III of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver Twist is confined to a dark and solitary room for a week after asking for more food. Despite his distress, he is not deprived of exercise, society, or religious consolation, but is instead subjected to harsh treatment such as being flogged and kicked into prayer. Mr. Gamfield, a chimney-sweep, sees a notice offering a boy for apprenticeship and approaches the board. After negotiations, the board agrees to give Gamfield three pounds ten for Oliver's apprenticeship. Before leaving, Gamfield warns Oliver to appear happy and cooperative. The magistrate, who is half-blind, is swayed by Oliver's appearance and asks him what is wrong. However, these details are not directly related to the events described in this chapter. ###

In Chapter IV of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver is offered a position as a cabin boy but is instead sent to live with Mr. Sowerberry, a parochial undertaker. Mr. Bumble, a parish beadle, arranges for Oliver to become an apprentice to Mr. Sowerberry after failing to secure a better position for him. Oliver is taken to Mr. Sowerberry's shop and then to the "kitchen," a damp and dark cellar where he is given a plate of leftover food. Despite his hunger, Oliver eats quickly and eagerly. Mrs. Sowerberry assigns Oliver to sleep in the cellar among the coffins, and he does so meekly. The chapter highlights Oliver's resilience and the harsh conditions he faces. ###

In Chapter V of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver and Mr. Bumble visit a poor family where a woman has died from starvation. The family, including a man, an old woman, and several children, are grieving but refuse to allow anyone to bury the woman, claiming she was starved to death. The undertaker measures the body and leaves, instructing the family to prepare for the burial. The next day, Mr. Bumble and Sowerberry bring four workhouse men to carry the woman to the graveyard. The burial is rushed, with the reverend completing the service quickly. The grave-digger then fills the grave, and the family departs, with the old woman complaining about losing her cloak. Oliver reflects on the grim scene as he returns to the shop. The chapter highlights the harsh realities faced by the poor and contrasts this with Oliver's new life with the Sowerberrys. ###

In Chapter VI of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver is formally apprenticed after a difficult month. He gains experience assisting at funerals, where he observes the stoic behavior of those who have lost loved ones. Despite this, Oliver remains meek under the abuse from Noah Claypole and Charlotte, who treat him poorly due to Noah's jealousy and Mrs. Sowerberry's dislike. One day, Noah taunts Oliver about his late mother, calling her "bad" and suggesting she deserved her fate. This provokes Oliver, who loses control and attacks Noah, knocking him to the ground. Charlotte and Mrs. Sowerberry intervene, and they lock Oliver in the dust cellar. Mrs. Sowerberry cries, while Noah is commiserated over. Noah is sent to fetch Mr. Bumble, and he runs through the streets without his cap, carrying a clasp-knife to reduce swelling from a black eye. The incident highlights Oliver's growing resilience and the harsh conditions he faces. ###

In Chapter VII of *Oliver Twist*, Noah Claypole runs to the workhouse to report that Oliver Twist has become "wicious" and attempted to murder several people, including Noah himself. Mr. Bumble, the beadle, is alarmed and sends him to get the gentleman in the white waistcoat, who orders Bumble to bring Oliver to Sowerberry's shop for punishment. Upon arrival, Mr. Bumble finds Oliver still kicking at the cellar door and overhears Mrs. Sowerberry and Charlotte discussing Oliver's behavior. Mr. Bumble suggests starving Oliver and putting him on gruel to tame his spirit. When Sowerberry returns, he punishes Oliver severely, believing his mother deserves the harsh words he used. Despite the abuse, Oliver remains defiant. Later, Oliver escapes from the shop and meets his childhood friend Dick, who is also being mistreated. Oliver leaves a parting blessing from Dick, which stays with him throughout his life.

In Chapter VIII of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver, after a grueling journey from the workhouse, finally arrives in London. He meets Jack Dawkins, known as "The Artful Dodger," who takes him to Fagin's hideout. Dawkins leads Oliver into a dark, dirty room where Fagin and several other boys are gathered. The room is sparsely furnished with a table, drinks, food, and beds. Fagin greets Oliver warmly and introduces him to the others. Initially, the boys are friendly, but Fagin discourages their familiarity using his toasting fork. After sharing a meal, Fagin offers Oliver a glass of gin and water, and Oliver falls asleep on one of the beds. ###

In Chapter IX of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver awakens late the next morning in the presence of the old Jew, who is preparing coffee. Despite appearing awake, Oliver is still somewhat drowsy and his mind wanders to memories of his past. The Jew, who has a collection of valuable jewelry, expresses satisfaction with the thieves he sent out to work. When Oliver accidentally observes the Jew's activities, the old man becomes suspicious and confronts him. After calming down, the Jew allows Oliver to get up and offers him a basin to wash in. The Dodger and Charley Bates return with stolen goods, and the group engages in a playful game where the Jew pretends to be an old gentleman walking in the street, while the boys steal from him. Two young women, Bet and Nancy, visit, and the group spends time socializing. The Jew advises Oliver to emulate the Dodger and Charley, and teaches him how to pickpocket. Oliver wonders about the connection between the game and his future prospects but follows the Jew's instructions. The chapter highlights the criminal lifestyle and the manipulation of Oliver by the older characters. ###

Oliver, after working with the Jew and his associates for several days, begins to long for fresh air and work outside. He is motivated by the strict moral teachings of the old gentleman, who often criticizes idleness and encourages an active lifestyle. One day, Oliver finally gets permission to join his companions, Charley Bates and the Dodger, in their work. They set out, but Oliver suspects they might be deceiving the old gentleman. Instead, they approach an elderly gentleman reading at a book stall and rob him of his handkerchief. Shocked, Oliver flees, pursued by the old gentleman and the two boys. The crowd quickly joins the chase, and Oliver is eventually caught by a police officer. Despite his protests that the Dodger and Charley Bates were the real culprits, Oliver is taken away, leaving the old gentleman to believe he was the thief. The chapter highlights Oliver's growing awareness of the criminal world and the dangers he faces. ###

This chapter describes the arrest and trial of Oliver Twist at a police station. The old gentleman, Mr. Brownlow, encounters a police magistrate named Mr. Fang, who is known for his harsh and unfair methods. Oliver is accused of stealing a handkerchief, but Mr. Brownlow doubts his guilt. After searching Oliver and finding nothing, he is locked in a dirty cell. Mr. Brownlow reflects on Oliver's face and recalls a similar expression from his past, but cannot remember where he saw it. When Mr. Brownlow tries to explain the situation to Mr. Fang, the magistrate becomes angry and demands evidence. The policeman testifies that he found nothing on Oliver and that there are no witnesses. Mr. Fang, in a fit of rage, threatens to punish Mr. Brownlow for disrespect, but is interrupted by the clerk and jailor. The chapter highlights the unfair treatment of Oliver and the potential injustice of the legal system. ###

chapters.summary: In a courtroom, Mr. Brownlow attempts to explain that Oliver, whom he believes to be innocent, was mistakenly accused of theft. Despite interruptions and insults from Mr. Fang, the magistrate, Mr. Brownlow insists that Oliver was hurt and possibly ill. Mr. Fang, however, dismisses these claims and demands Oliver's name. When Oliver fails to respond, the officer guesses "Tom White." Mr. Brownlow adds that Oliver's parents died in infancy. Oliver then faints due to thirst, prompting Mr. Fang to mock him. Mr. Fang decides to commit Oliver to hard labor for three months. Just as Oliver is about to be taken away, an elderly bookstall keeper rushes in, claiming he witnessed the incident and saw Oliver was not involved in the theft. Despite Mr. Fang's objections, the bookstall keeper is sworn in and explains that he saw Oliver was amazed by the crime. Mr. Fang then dismisses Mr. Brownlow and the bookstall keeper, releasing Oliver. Mr. Brownlow, enraged, leaves with the book and takes Oliver to a coach for medical attention. ###

In Chapter XII of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver is taken to a new home where he receives better care than he ever had before. A kind old lady named Mrs. Bedwin tends to him with great compassion. For several days, Oliver remains unconscious due to a severe fever. When he finally regains consciousness, he asks where he is and expresses confusion about his surroundings. Mrs. Bedwin comforts him and reassures him that he is safe. Oliver, in a poignant moment, reflects on his mother and wonders if she is watching over him from heaven. Mrs. Bedwin, moved by his gratitude, wipes away her tears and acknowledges the fever's effect on his perception. Despite his delirium, Oliver maintains a sense of hope and love for his mother, even though he knows she cannot see him. The chapter highlights the contrast between Oliver's previous harsh treatment and the tender care he now receives. ###

chapters.summary: Oliver, after being tended to by a kind old lady named Mrs. Bedwin, begins to recover from his illness. The doctor visits and confirms that Oliver is improving. Oliver falls asleep and dreams about a portrait that seems to follow him. When he wakes, he feels much better and Mrs. Bedwin starts to cry with joy. Mr. Brownlow, Oliver's benefactor, arrives and is moved by Oliver's appearance. Oliver explains that his name is Oliver Twist, not White, which surprises Mr. Brownlow. Upon seeing a portrait of a woman with similar features to Oliver, Mr. Brownlow becomes curious and concerned. Oliver faints, and the narrative reveals that the Dodger and Charley Bates, who had previously stolen from Mr. Brownlow, had been pursuing Oliver. They flee when Mr. Brownlow's attention is drawn to Oliver, and they return to Fagin. Mr. Brownlow's reaction to Oliver's resemblance to the portrait suggests that Oliver might be related to someone important. The chapter ends with the Dodger and Charley Bates returning to Fagin. ###

In Chapter XIII of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. Fagin confronts the young thieves, the Dodger and Charley Bates, about Oliver's whereabouts. The Dodger initially claims Oliver was caught by "the traps" (police), but when Mr. Fagin threatens him, the Dodger pulls a toasting fork to defend himself. Mr. Fagin's associate, Bill Sikes, enters and demands to know what happened. Sikes becomes suspicious of Fagin's behavior and accuses him of mishandling the situation. Fagin tries to reassure Sikes but is interrupted by the arrival of two young women, one of whom, Nancy, agrees to go to the police station to find out information about Oliver. Despite initial reluctance, Nancy eventually agrees to help. Sikes and the others leave to search for Oliver, with Fagin promising to provide money and support. The chapter ends with Fagin expressing concern that Oliver might still be in danger and considering ways to silence him if necessary.

In Chapter XIV of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver recovers from a fainting spell at Mr. Brownlow's house and is given a new suit of clothes. He enjoys playing cribbage with Mrs. Bedwin and discussing reading and writing with Mr. Brownlow, who reassures him he won't become an author. Mr. Grimwig, an old friend of Mr. Brownlow, arrives unexpectedly and questions Oliver about his past, including the origin of an orange peel found on the staircase. Despite Mr. Grimwig's skepticism, Mr. Brownlow remains patient and accommodating. Later, Mr. Brownlow plans to hear Oliver's story the next morning, while Mr. Grimwig doubts Oliver's honesty and suggests testing him by having him return books to a bookstall-keeper. Oliver successfully completes the task, but Mr. Grimwig still harbors doubts. The chapter ends with the two men waiting in silence for Oliver to return, reflecting their differing hopes and determination. ###

In a dimly lit, squalid pub in Little Saffron Hill, Bill Sikes, a criminal, is brooding over a drink while his dog, which has injured him, growls and bites at him. When Fagin enters, Sikes accuses him of not hearing the commotion. Fagin explains that he didn't hear anything and offers Sikes money from a job, which Sikes demands immediately. After Sikes leaves, Nancy arrives, and Sikes recognizes her. She explains that she's found Oliver Twist and tries to take him home, but Oliver protests that he doesn't know her. A man who claims to be Oliver's brother appears, and Sikes identifies Nancy as the woman who found Oliver. Sikes takes Oliver, and despite Nancy's pleas, forces him into a dark alley with his dog. The scene ends with Oliver being dragged away, and the others waiting anxiously for news of him. ###

In Chapter XVI of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver, Sikes, and Nancy meet at a secret location in Smithfield where Fagin and his gang are waiting. Sikes demands the five-pound note that Nancy stole, leading to a dispute. Oliver kneels before Fagin, begging to return the books and money to the gentleman who had taken care of him, which angers Sikes. Nancy intervenes, warning Fagin and Sikes that she will harm them if they continue to mistreat Oliver. Nancy becomes angry and faints after an argument with Sikes, who accuses her of being a thief and a bad influence on Oliver. Fagin tries to calm the situation, and Charley shows Oliver to bed. The chapter ends with the sounds of laughter and Nancy's friend arriving to help her recover. ###

He is greeted warmly at Mrs. Mann's farm but maintains a dignified demeanor. Mrs. Mann provides him with his monthly stipend and updates on the children, including a sickly boy named Dick, who expresses a wish to leave a message for Oliver Twist. Mr. Bumble conveys this information to Mr. Brownlow, who offers a reward for information about Oliver's whereabouts. Despite Mrs. Bedwin's defense of Oliver, Mr. Brownlow remains convinced of his guilt. Mr. Bumble leaves with the reward money, and Mr. Brownlow, upset by the beadle's account, declares that Oliver is an imposter. Mrs. Bedwin strongly defends Oliver, stating he was kind and gentle, but Mr. Brownlow, feigning anger, orders her to leave. This news saddens Oliver's friends, including Oliver himself, who feels despondent upon learning of the accusations against him. ### Instruction: Combine the following summaries into one coherent summary.

The boys, including Tom Chitling and Charley Bates, mock Oliver and make jokes about him joining their gang. Fagin reassures Oliver and speaks positively about the benefits of their trade, highlighting the skills of the Dodger and the amiability of Charley Bates. He also emphasizes his own generosity. As the group discusses their activities, Fagin tells stories that amuse Oliver despite his reservations. Over time, Fagin gradually influences Oliver, preparing him to embrace their lifestyle by offering companionship and entertainment, while subtly poisoning his mind with criminal values. Fagin expresses concern for Oliver's future and warns him about the discomforts of hanging. Oliver spends several days isolated, reflecting on his friends and feeling guilty. In Chapter XIX of "Oliver Twist," the Jewish character, Mr. Fagin, leaves his den late at night, dressed warmly and cautiously, heading towards Spitalfields. He arrives at a house in Bethnal Green where he meets Nancy, a young woman who has previously helped Oliver. They enter a poorly-furnished room where Sikes, another criminal, is waiting. Sikes demands to know about a planned robbery at Chertsey, which Fagin and Toby Crackit had intended to execute. Sikes reveals that Toby has failed to infiltrate the household due to the long-term loyalty of the residents. Despite this setback, Fagin remains determined and agrees to attempt the robbery from the outside if it can be done safely. chapters.summary: In this excerpt from "Oliver Twist," Mr. Fagin and Mr. Sikes discuss plans to kidnap Oliver Twist and use him for their criminal activities. They decide to wait until after the next full moon to carry out the plan. Fagin and Sikes arrange for Nancy to bring Oliver to Fagin's hideout the following evening. Fagin emphasizes that he will have complete control over Oliver and that Sikes will not be held responsible for any harm that comes to him. Sikes expresses his willingness to use force if necessary. After making these arrangements, Sikes becomes intoxicated and falls asleep with a box of housebreaking tools. Fagin leaves, reflecting on the reliability of women and his plan to exploit Oliver. The chapter ends with a description of Oliver, who is sleeping on a crude bed, looking pale and sad due to his recent experiences. ###

In Chapter XX of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver wakes up to find new shoes at his bedside but is soon informed he is to be taken to Mr. William Sikes' residence that night. Fagin reassures Oliver that he will return, warning him to be cautious around Sikes, who is described as violent. Nancy visits Oliver, insisting he must accompany her despite his reluctance. She warns him to remain silent and to follow her instructions, revealing that Sikes intends to use Oliver for a dangerous task. Nancy helps Oliver escape and they flee to Sikes' house. Upon arrival, Sikes gives Oliver a lecture about staying silent and the consequences of speaking, emphasizing the use of violence if necessary. Nancy prepares breakfast as Sikes gets ready to leave, and Oliver is taken out by Sikes, leaving the girl behind. The chapter ends with Oliver and Sikes heading out into the rainy night, while Nancy sits quietly by the fire. ###

In Chapter XXI of *Oliver Twist*, Oliver and Mr. Sikes set out on a journey on a dreary morning. They navigate through various London streets, encountering a bustling market in Smithfield before continuing to Isleworth. Sikes asks a cart driver for a lift, and they eventually reach Hampton. They spend several hours in the countryside, stopping at a public house for dinner. After eating, they continue their journey under cover of darkness, stopping at a dilapidated house near Shepperton. Sikes leads Oliver inside, and they wait in silence, with Oliver fearing the worst. The chapter ends with them inside the abandoned house.

In Chapter XXII of *Oliver Twist*, Bill Sikes and Toby Crackit, along with Barney, plan and execute a burglary. Sikes brings Oliver, a young boy, to assist them. They enter a dark, smoky room where Sikes and Crackit are waiting. Crackit, a small, red-haired man, recognizes Oliver as Fagin's boy and comments on his potential value for theft. Sikes orders Oliver to drink alcohol, which he reluctantly does, causing him to cough violently. After a brief nap, they prepare to leave. They cross a bridge and head towards Chertsey, where they plan to break into a house. Sikes and Crackit climb over a wall, and Sikes uses a crowbar to open a small window. He instructs Oliver to enter the house and unlock the street door. Despite his fear, Oliver attempts to flee but is caught by Sikes, who fires a warning shot. Sikes and Oliver return to the wall, and Sikes drags him back into the house. They are interrupted by a disturbance, and Sikes fires a shot, dragging Oliver back through the window. The sound of alarms and gunfire ensues, and Sikes carries Oliver away, noting that he has been hit. The chapter ends with the sounds of chaos growing distant, and Oliver losing consciousness.

In Chapter XXIII of *Oliver Twist*, Mrs. Corney, the matron of a workhouse, reflects on her situation while preparing tea. The weather is harsh and cold, and Mrs. Corney feels grateful for her comfortable home. However, she becomes upset when a small teapot spills, scalding her hand. Mr. Bumble, the beadle, arrives unexpectedly and begins a conversation with Mrs. Corney, complaining about the ungrateful behavior of the paupers who receive relief. Mrs. Corney agrees with his views and discusses the inefficacy of outdoor relief. Mr. Bumble then brings a gift of port wine for the infirmary and offers to share a cup of tea with Mrs. Corney. They chat about cats and kittens, and Mr. Bumble makes a suggestive move, causing Mrs. Corney to react with alarm. Just as things become tense, an old woman arrives to inform Mrs. Corney that Old Sally, a pauper, is dying and has something important to tell her. Mrs. Corney leaves to attend to the situation, and Mr. Bumble engages in peculiar behavior, including counting utensils and dancing around the table. The chapter ends with Mr. Bumble seemingly inventorying the furniture.

In Chapter XXIV of *Oliver Twist*, the matron visits a dying woman in a poorhouse. The woman, suffering from illness, is near death and reveals that she once stole a piece of gold from a young woman who had given birth to a child and died. The gold, which the woman believed might have saved the mother's life, was stolen because the mother had trusted her with it. The dying woman mentions that the child, named Oliver, looked like his mother and that she felt responsible for his death. After making these revelations, the woman dies. The matron dismisses the old women who were listening and leaves, showing little concern. The old women remain, preparing for their grim tasks. ###

In Chapter XXV of "Oliver Twist," Mr. Fagin is brooding in his den while his gang, including the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling, plays whist. The Dodger takes dummy, and Bates frequently drinks gin and makes jokes, despite losing consistently. Mr. Chitling loses money but finds humor in it. Fagin overhears a conversation about Mr. Chitling's infatuation with Betsy, which amuses Bates. When the Dodger hears a tinkler's bell, he goes upstairs, returning with Toby Crackit, a housebreaker. Toby explains that a robbery attempt failed because they were fired upon, and they left the injured boy behind. Fagin reacts with distress and leaves the house. The chapter captures the dynamics and tensions within Fagin's criminal group. ###

In Chapter XXVI of *Oliver Twist*, Fagin, after escaping from Toby Crackit, finds himself in Field Lane and proceeds to "The Three Cripples," where he learns that Monks is expected soon. Fagin meets Nancy, who is drunk and conflicted about her involvement with him and the boys. Fagin pressures Nancy to agree to kill Monks if Barney returns with the boy, and despite her resolute and dismissive attitude due to her intoxication, Fagin leaves satisfied that she is too drunk to pose a threat. He then goes to Sikes' residence in Bethnal Green. Later, Fagin returns to his den to find Nancy still asleep at the table. He meets Monks, who accuses Fagin of not following through with a plan to keep Oliver Twist as a pickpocket

In Chapter XXVII of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. Bumble, the beadle, returns to Mrs. Corney's chambers to find her distressed and in need of comfort. After she recovers with a dose of peppermint medicine, Mr. Bumble and Mrs. Corney discuss her recent loss and the possibility of a romantic relationship. They agree to marry, and their engagement is sealed with another dose of the medicine. Mr. Bumble then visits Noah Claypole and Charlotte at the undertaker's shop, where he discovers Noah is intoxicated and Charlotte is kissing him. Mr. Bumble intervenes, scolding them and ordering Noah to close the shop. The chapter concludes with a brief mention of preparing for the old woman's funeral and setting out to find young Oliver Twist. ###

In Chapter XXVIII of *Oliver Twist*, Sikes and Toby Crackit chase Oliver after his escape from Fagin's gang, but Sikes leaves him unconscious in a ditch. Upon returning to the scene of the attempted robbery, Mr. Giles and his companions find Oliver lying injured. Mr. Giles, suspecting Oliver to be a thief, drags him into the house. The women servants are summoned, and a young lady directs that Oliver be taken to Mr. Giles's room while sending Brittles to fetch a constable and doctor. Despite Mr. Giles's insistence, the young lady refuses to see Oliver herself, asking that he be treated kindly for her sake. In a well-furnished room, two ladies are having breakfast. The older lady, Mrs. Maylie, is seated in a high-backed chair, dressed in a mix of old and new styles. Her young companion, Rose, is in her late teens, described as pure and beautiful. Mr. Giles, dressed formally in black, stands nearby, looking important. After a long absence, Dr. Losberne returns and reveals that a boy was shot during the incident. Despite initial reluctance, Mrs. Maylie agrees to see the injured boy in Dr. Losberne's presence. ###

In Chapter XXX of *Oliver Twist*, Dr. Losberne and two ladies visit Oliver, who is recovering in a bedroom. Initially, they are surprised to find a young, injured boy rather than the expected criminal. They discuss Oliver's condition and consider his background, suspecting he might have been involved with criminals due to his young age and lack of a home. Rose, one of the ladies, pleads with Dr. Losberne to spare Oliver from imprisonment, emphasizing his innocence and vulnerability. Dr. Losberne agrees to try to negotiate with Oliver's captors, Mr. Giles and Mr. Brittles, to avoid immediate punishment, provided he can examine Oliver and determine his character. In Chapter XXXI of *Oliver Twist*, Mr. Losberne and his guests are visited by two police officers, Mr. Blathers and Mr. Duff, who are investigating an attempted robbery at the Maylie residence. The officers question the servants and examine the scene, finding that the attempted robbery was likely committed by a town hand rather than a countryman. They also discover that the boy mentioned by the servants as being involved in the attempted robbery was not actually involved. Mr. Blathers shares a similar case involving a public-house owner named Conkey Chickweed, who was accused of false alarms. The officers suggest giving the boy some spirits to calm him.
